_meta.model: claude-sonnet-4-6 (MODELS.SMART), 2 parallel calls (arc + mechanics) merged, + 1 FAST v2 guard check/repair, + a 10s keep-alive heartbeat
_meta.how_to_regression_diff: Re-run (npm run check:golden party-architect). PARTY ARCHITECT REWRITE INSTRUCTIONS pass, 2026-09-05: full schema replacement. Old schema (energy_curve, mixing_strategies, conversation_starters, food_and_drink_strategy, music_plan, the_exit, budget_breakdown, disaster_prevention) is GONE — do not resurrect those keys. New: event_read{what_matters,design_priority}, event_shape (pacing STRATEGY, never a feelings prediction), timeline[]{time,phase,action,host_job,why,adjust_if} with RELATIVE time offsets only (Arrival/+20 min/Around halfway/Final 45 min — never a clock time, since this form collects no start time), helping_people_connect[] (was mixing_strategies, 0-3, no forced count), conversation_catalysts[] (0-3), food_and_drink{format,timing,dietary_considerations,special_touch} (dietary_considerations must be procedural — 'identify/separate/label' — never a safety ASSURANCE like 'will keep guests safe'), music{show,arrival,later,wind_down} (show=false + empty fields when irrelevant), budget_priorities{approach,protect_spending_on[],keep_secondary[],use_what_you_have[]} (priorities, never a fabricated total or a 'budget is workable' verdict), things_to_plan_for[] (was disaster_prevention, 0-4, grounded only in supplied facts, never a predicted future event), wind_down{signals[],script} (top-level — DIFFERENT from music.wind_down, which is about lowering volume). Uses router.outputStandard='v2' + runOutputGuard (prohibit/require list) instead of the old bare toArray()-coerce with no guard. IMPORTANT GOTCHA FIXED THIS PASS: the guard's own repair sometimes blanks a flagged field to '' when it can't produce a clean rewrite (observed live on conversation_catalysts and budget_priorities.protect_spending_on) — outputGuard's requiredNonEmpty only protects a fixed known-in-advance path, not a dynamically-indexed array item, so party-architect.js adds its own pruneEmpties() pass AFTER the guard to drop any blanked plain-string array item or object-array item whose primary field (how/plan/action+host_job) came back blank. DO NOT remove pruneEmpties — it is the only thing standing between a guard repair and a visible blank line/empty bullet in production. Case 1 (housewarming) is a guard PASS with zero violations on this run — case 2 (40th birthday) exercises a guard FAIL-then-repair cycle (7 fields, all successfully rewritten with real content, none needed pruning on this particular run, but the dietary_considerations field is the reference for the 'never a safety assurance' fix — compare it against the pre-fix version in git history, which said a labeling setup 'will keep guests safe'). Frontend Recent Plans is a NEW store (`party-plans`, full inputs+plan+date) — the old `party-history` store (preview-only) stays read-only/legacy, same migration pattern as Small Change Big Difference's Recent Small Changes. GENERAL REASONING & GROUNDING RULES pass (2026-09-05, second same-day pass): SHARED_PROMPT was fully replaced (not appended to) with a 25-section grounding spec supplied whole by the user — output schema, arc/mechanics split, and each half's own schema-mechanics (item counts, field names) are UNCHANGED. Both cases re-recorded against the new prompt (output content differs from the prior baseline; structure does not). Also added this same day: a keep-alive heartbeat in the route handler (res.write(' ') every 10s while the two parallel generations + guard run) after a live report of "NetworkError when attempting to fetch resource" at 43s on a non-streaming request — this tool already had documented history of tripping a browser/proxy idle-timeout at this shape (the original pre-split version measured ~82s). Verified: (1) the heartbeat's leading whitespace bytes don't break JSON.parse/response.json() — confirmed via a real browser test, not just Node's http client; (2) an error occurring AFTER the heartbeat has already committed the HTTP status to 200 is still surfaced correctly, via a matching change in src/hooks/useClaudeAPI.js's callToolEndpoint (checks for a bare single-key {error} body even on a 200 response) — verified with a temporary forced-error test exercising exactly that path, then reverted. DO NOT remove the keep-alive or the useClaudeAPI.js check together — removing one without the other reopens either the timeout bug or the silent-blank-result bug. FINAL GENERAL PROMPT CORRECTIONS pass (2026-09-05, third same-day pass): 18 more sections ADDED (not replacing) to SHARED_PROMPT — §26-43 plus a closing FINAL OPERATING RULE, all before FINAL NORTH STAR. These target failures the first grounding pass still let through on live review of this exact housewarming case: inventing relationship topology between guest groups beyond what was supplied (§26), fabricating introduction content — jobs/hometowns/backstory (§27), manufacturing a midpoint shared moment without an established need (§28 — the schema's 'Shared Moment' timeline phase must now be genuinely optional, see case 1/case 2's own adjust_if fields), claiming a planned element already 'landed' or 'worked' (§29), diagnosing ordinary quiet/standing behavior as a problem (§30), manufacturing conversational value for ordinary objects/food (§31), inventing a psychological effect of music (§32 — this is the exact category the v2 guard fired on twice in the case 1 live test, both repaired cleanly), unsupported quantity/sufficiency claims and invented purchase-value claims in budget (§33-34), assuming standing duration from a seating-capacity gap (§35), expanding a supplied noise rule beyond its literal wording (§36), ranking who is 'most affected' without support (§37), inventing guest arrival/departure order (§38), using cleanup as a covert end-of-party signal rather than a practical step (§39 — case 2's timeline explicitly says cleanup is 'a practical step, not a signal'), forcing conversation_catalysts to be non-empty (§40), a logistical/social-opportunity/social-prediction classification test (§41), an inference-chain-length limit (§42), and a final 'what problem am I solving' generation test (§43). router.outputGuard gained 11 new prohibit categories matching the most mechanically-checkable of these (e.g. invented_psychological_effect_of_music, claimed_design_element_already_succeeded) — both golden cases exercised several of them live (guard FAILED then repaired 3 fields on each case; check the git history for this file's pre-repair content if you need the negative example). Case 1's input gained the visitor's own 'Nobody knows anybody outside their own pair' sentence (it was in the original bug report's scenario and is a SUPPLIED fact, not one the model should be inventing — §26 governs going BEYOND it, e.g. asserting coworkers-among-themselves don't know each other, not the supplied sentence itself).

input.whoIsComing: Three couples from my old job, my brother, and the neighbours from downstairs who I have spoken to twice. Nobody knows anybody outside their own pair.
input.space: One-bed flat. Living room seats five if two people take the floor. Kitchen is a corridor. No outdoor space.
input.constraints: Building has a noise rule after 10pm and thin floors. Nine people is already more than the room comfortably holds.

helping_people_connect.how: When each pair arrives, introduce them briefly to whoever is already there by name and how you know each person — nothing more unless you have a genuine connection to mention.
helping_people_connect.when: As each pair arrives, before they settle.
helping_people_connect.why_it_fits: With nine people in a small flat and no existing connections across groups, a name and a context ('from the old job,' 'my neighbours downstairs') are the facts available to introduce people.

conversation_catalysts: The flat itself — what you kept, what you got rid of, what you are still figuring out — is a ready topic at a housewarming that requires nothing to set up.

If you already have anything in the flat that has a story attached to it — a piece of furniture, artwork, or an object from somewhere — it can be talked about if someone asks, without needing to stage it as a prompt.

food_and_drink.format: Grazing, with everything laid out before the first guest arrives. A corridor kitchen makes serving individual portions from in there impractical, and a self-serve spread means you are not stuck in the kitchen for the first half of the gathering.
food_and_drink.timing: Have food available from the moment people arrive so there is no waiting period and no serving moment that interrupts early conversation. Replenish from the kitchen as needed rather than doing a single big reveal.
food_and_drink.special_touch: One drink that feels slightly deliberate — a simple punch, a specific beer, or a non-alcoholic option you made rather than bought — can mark the occasion without adding much effort or cost, if that appeals to you.

music.arrival: Keep it quiet enough that people do not have to raise their voices — the flat is small and sound will build quickly once nine people are talking. Background level only.
music.later: Once the room is full, consider turning it down further or off entirely. In a one-bed flat at capacity, music competes with conversation and adds to overall noise.
music.wind_down: Lower or stop music before the building noise rule applies — this also reduces the overall sound level at a point when the gathering is naturally entering its final phase.

budget_priorities.approach: With $120 and nine guests, decide on food and drink first, since those are the only practical expenses that directly affect all nine people. Anything left can go toward optional extras.
protect_spending_on: Enough food for nine people to graze across roughly three hours.
Drinks, including at least one non-alcoholic option, since you cannot know in advance what people do and do not drink.
keep_secondary: Decorative or occasion-specific items — the flat being new is the occasion, and it does not need to be dressed for the event.
use_what_you_have: If you already have serving dishes, use them rather than buying disposables.
If you have a speaker, it covers music at no cost.
If you have floor cushions, extra chairs, or a folding chair available, bring them out — the seating gap is real and worth closing before guests arrive.

things_to_plan_for.issue: The described space does not comfortably seat all nine guests at once, and the gap between available seating and guest count is significant.
things_to_plan_for.plan: Decide before the gathering whether you want to supplement seating — borrowed chairs, floor cushions — or treat it as a stand-and-move gathering from the start, so you are not improvising once people arrive.

things_to_plan_for.issue: The corridor kitchen limits how much you can do in there while people are present.
things_to_plan_for.plan: Have everything set out and ready before anyone arrives so the kitchen is only needed for replenishing, not for active hosting.

things_to_plan_for.issue: You said the building has a noise rule after 10pm and thin floors.
things_to_plan_for.plan: Know when your gathering started relative to that limit, and plan to reduce avoidable noise — music, volume of activity — before that point rather than at it.

things_to_plan_for.issue: The neighbours from downstairs are guests, which means the usual option of accepting some downstairs noise complaints does not apply.
things_to_plan_for.plan: Know when your gathering started relative to the 10pm noise limit, and plan to reduce avoidable noise — music, volume of activity — before that point rather than at it.

event_read.what_matters: Nine people in a one-bed flat with corridor kitchen and five-seat living room means the physical setup is the central design problem — not the social one. The neighbours are a genuine wildcard only in the sense that they are less familiar to you; that is worth one deliberate introduction, not a structural intervention.
event_read.design_priority: Keep the host free from continuous room management so the gathering can run on conversation and comfort rather than coordination.

output.event_shape: Let arrival be slow and unstructured — people finding spots, drinks in hand, no moment where everyone is expected to do the same thing at once. Around halfway, if it feels right, make one brief occasion of the housewarming itself — something simple that acknowledges the new place — then return to open time. The final stretch needs no new activity; the host simply stops introducing anything new and lets the evening find its own level before wrapping up directly.

timeline.action: Have drinks accessible immediately — on a surface guests can reach themselves — so no one is waiting to be served and the corridor kitchen stays clear.
timeline.host_job: Welcome each arrival, introduce the neighbours by name and how you know them since they are the least-connected guests, then step back.
timeline.why: Self-serve removes a repeated logistical trip through a corridor kitchen and means you are not stuck in there while guests are arriving.
timeline.adjust_if: If the neighbours arrive before any of the work couples, spend a few more minutes with them until another guest arrives who you can fold them into.

timeline.action: Nothing new. Let people settle — standing, sitting on the floor, wherever they land. Food if you are serving it can come out now or was already accessible.
timeline.host_job: Move around the room naturally. Make any remaining introductions where you know a genuine point of connection; otherwise names and context are enough.
timeline.why: The room is small and will feel full. The plan at this point is simply to not add any new demands on it.

timeline.action: If you want one brief occasion moment — a short toast to the new flat, a thank-you for coming — do it here. Keep it under a minute. This is optional: skip it if conversation is already running well and an interruption would cost more than it adds.
timeline.host_job: Say the thing simply and briefly, then return to the room. Do not extend it.
timeline.why: A housewarming has a natural occasion built in. A brief acknowledgment takes under a minute and lets you return to the room immediately.
timeline.adjust_if: If it feels unnecessary or the moment does not present itself naturally, leave it out entirely. The gathering does not require it.

timeline.action: Nothing new. Stop introducing any activities or topics. If food is largely done, consolidate what remains rather than replenishing.
timeline.host_job: Enjoy the gathering. You do not need to manage the room at this point.
timeline.why: Adding anything new this late extends the event past its natural close and increases the risk of running into the noise constraint.

timeline.action: Begin saying goodnight to guests who are already making moves to leave. Do any light, practical tidying — collecting empty cups, consolidating bottles — because it needs doing regardless.
timeline.host_job: Be warm and direct. If the event needs to end by a particular point because of the noise rule, say so clearly rather than hoping the room reads environmental signals.
timeline.why: A small flat with a noise constraint needs a clear ending, not a gradual one managed through atmosphere.
timeline.adjust_if: If guests are already gathering coats and wrapping up naturally, you may not need to say anything beyond goodbye.

signals: Stop replenishing food and drinks — consolidate what is left rather than opening anything new.
Begin saying proper goodbyes to the first guests who move toward leaving, which naturally brings the evening to a close.
If the noise constraint is approaching and the room is still lively, name it directly rather than hoping people infer it.
wind_down.script: This has been really lovely — thank you all for coming to see the place. I should start winding things down, partly because of the building noise rule, but mostly because it is getting late. So glad you came.

input.whoIsComing: Mostly close friends from the last 15 years, a few work people, 3 kids under 10. About a third haven't met each other.
input.space: Backyard with covered patio, fits ~25 standing. Kitchen and living room flow out to it. Late September — should be warm but cool by 9pm.
input.constraints: Two guests have tree nut allergies, one is gluten-free, one is sober (they're fine with others drinking).

helping_people_connect.how: When you greet arriving guests, briefly introduce them to whoever is nearby using names and how you know each person — nothing more unless you know a genuine point of connection.
helping_people_connect.when: As each guest arrives, during the first part of the gathering.
helping_people_connect.why_it_fits: About a third of the 22 guests haven't met each other, and arrivals are a natural moment to make introductions without interrupting ongoing conversations.

helping_people_connect.idea: Keep the space open between inside and outside.
helping_people_connect.how: Leave the kitchen-to-backyard flow unobstructed so guests move between areas naturally rather than settling into fixed clusters.
helping_people_connect.why_it_fits: The indoor-outdoor layout means guests can move between areas naturally without clustering in one spot, and the kitchen-to-backyard flow makes that easy to do.

conversation_catalysts: Leave the space unstructured. Guests will naturally gravitate toward conversation and the food and drinks available to them.

food_and_drink.format: Grazing-style — food set out for guests to help themselves. With 22 people across an indoor-outdoor space and a relaxed vibe, this avoids a serving bottleneck, keeps the host out of a serving role, and suits a four-hour gathering where people arrive and move around.
food_and_drink.timing: Have food available from the moment guests start arriving rather than at a designated serving moment. With kids in attendance and a four-hour window, having something out immediately reduces wait and keeps the gathering low-maintenance from the start.
food_and_drink.dietary_considerations: Two guests have tree nut allergies — keep tree nuts out of shared dishes entirely rather than labeling around them, since cross-contact on a grazing table is hard to control. One guest is gluten-free — label gluten-containing items clearly and make sure at least a few dishes are naturally gluten-free and clearly identified as such. One guest is sober — have appealing non-alcoholic options available from the start alongside any alcohol, not as an afterthought.
food_and_drink.special_touch: A dedicated non-alcoholic drink option that's a bit more considered than water or soda — a simple fruit-based punch, a sparkling mocktail, or a make-your-own spritzer setup if you're up for it. It serves the sober guest without singling them out and gives everyone an alternative.

music.arrival: Keep music present but at a volume where guests don't need to raise their voices — the purpose at this stage is to fill silence, not to set a performance tone.
music.later: You can let the volume or tempo shift slightly as the gathering fills out and conversation is carrying itself, but keep it low enough that people across the patio can still talk easily.
music.wind_down: As the gathering moves toward its end and you expect it to cool down after a few hours, lowering the volume gradually is a simple way to reduce the overall sound level without an abrupt change — useful given the late-evening temperature shift may already be moving people indoors.

budget_priorities.approach: With 22 guests over four hours, food and drink will be the most variable cost — plan that first and let everything else follow from what remains. Dietary constraints here are hard constraints, not preferences, so reliable labeling and safe food handling are part of that core spend, not optional extras.
protect_spending_on: Food and grazing spread — enough variety to cover the dietary constraints without making the constrained guests feel like an afterthought.
Drinks — including a considered non-alcoholic option alongside whatever else you're offering.
Any rental or borrowing needed if your current setup doesn't seat or serve 22 comfortably across the indoor-outdoor space.
keep_secondary: Decorations — the backyard and covered patio described are already a setting; decor is optional at a relaxed gathering.
Activity or game equipment — only worth spending on if the group specifically calls for it.
use_what_you_have: If you already have serving platters, coolers, or a drinks station of some kind, use those before buying anything new.
If you have outdoor lighting already — string lights, lanterns, or otherwise — have it ready to switch on as it cools and gets darker toward the end of the evening.
If you have a speaker, use it; this gathering doesn't call for anything more than that.

things_to_plan_for.issue: The covered patio fits around 25 standing, but the full guest list is 22 — so if guests are spread across the patio, kitchen, and living room at different times, the patio alone may feel at or near capacity during peak moments.
things_to_plan_for.plan: Decide in advance whether the kitchen and living room are genuinely usable overflow space or just passthrough — if they're usable, make that clear by having drinks or food accessible there too, not only outside.

things_to_plan_for.issue: Late September with an expected temperature drop around the later part of the evening means the outdoor setup may become uncomfortable for some guests before the gathering ends.
things_to_plan_for.plan: Have a plan for what happens when it cools — whether that's moving the core of the party indoors, having something warm available to drink, or simply accepting that some guests may drift inside as the temperature drops.

things_to_plan_for.issue: Three children under 10 are attending a four-hour evening gathering.
things_to_plan_for.plan: Check in with the parents about what those kids will need — whether that's a quieter indoor spot, something to do, or simply knowing where the bathroom is — rather than building assumptions about it into the plan.

things_to_plan_for.issue: Tree nut allergies require more than labeling on a shared grazing table — cross-contact between dishes is a real consideration.
things_to_plan_for.plan: Decide before shopping whether to make the entire spread tree-nut-free (simpler and safer) or to keep nut-containing items physically separate with dedicated serving utensils — and communicate whichever approach you choose to those guests directly.

event_read.what_matters: About a third of 22 guests haven't met each other, so the design needs to make it easy for people to move and talk without requiring the host to actively manage introductions all night. The covered patio is the natural center, but the kitchen and living room create useful overflow that prevents the space from feeling crowded.
event_read.design_priority: Keep the host present and relaxed, not orchestrating — the setup should do most of the work.

output.event_shape: Let the first stretch be purely arrival and settling: food and drinks available from the start, no structured moments, no host announcements. Around the midpoint, if it feels right, mark the birthday briefly — a toast or a simple 'glad you're all here' moment — then return to open conversation for the rest of the event. As the weather cools later on, the indoor spaces become a natural extension rather than a fallback. The plan has one optional focal point and otherwise stays out of the way.

timeline.action: Food and drinks fully set out before the first guest arrives. Dietary-safe options clearly labeled for the tree nut and gluten-free constraints. The sober guest should have at least one appealing non-alcoholic option, not just water.
timeline.host_job: Welcome people as they arrive, point them toward food and drinks, make introductions where you know a useful connection exists.
timeline.why: Removing any wait for food or drink means the host doesn't need to manage a serving moment during the busiest part of arrival.

timeline.action: Nothing new to introduce. Let food, drinks, and conversation continue. The patio, kitchen, and living room are all open — people can find their own comfortable spots.
timeline.host_job: Stop managing arrivals and join the gathering. Make any remaining introductions that seem genuinely useful, then let it run.
timeline.why: By this point most guests who plan to arrive early will have arrived. The host's job shifts from logistics to presence.
timeline.adjust_if: If people are still arriving steadily, stay in arrival mode a little longer before stepping back.

timeline.action: One brief birthday acknowledgment — a short toast, a simple 'thanks for being here,' or whatever fits the birthday person's preference. Keep it under two minutes. This is optional: if the night is already going well and a pause would interrupt rather than add anything, skip it.
timeline.host_job: If you want this moment, gather loose attention, say something brief and genuine, and move on. No need to corral everyone into one spot.
timeline.why: A 40th birthday is a reason people gathered — one small acknowledgment of that is available if it fits. It is not required.
timeline.adjust_if: If conversation is running well and a pause feels like an interruption, leave it out entirely.

timeline.action: Return immediately to open, unstructured time. No new activities. Replenish food and drinks if needed.
timeline.host_job: Be a guest at your own party. Check food levels once, handle anything practical that needs handling, otherwise enjoy it.
timeline.why: The longest stretch of the evening should have the least host involvement. If the setup is working, there is nothing to manage.

timeline.action: Stop introducing anything new. If the temperature has dropped and people are moving indoors, let that happen naturally. Begin light cleanup of finished items — empty platters, used cups — as a practical step, not as a signal.
timeline.host_job: Stay present and social. Do not disappear into cleanup. Remove finished items when convenient, not continuously.
timeline.why: Reducing available food and tidying finished items is practical end-of-event maintenance, not a behavioral nudge.
timeline.adjust_if: If the group is still going strong and the planned end time is not a hard constraint, there is no reason to intervene.

timeline.action: Say clearly and warmly that the night is wrapping up. Thank people directly. Say goodbye to guests as they leave.
timeline.host_job: Be explicit that the event is ending — no need to hint. Personal goodbyes are the close.
timeline.why: Clarity is kinder than ambiguity. A direct, warm close is enough.

signals: Say directly and warmly that the night is winding down — no need to imply it.
Stop replenishing food and consolidate what remains to one area.
Begin saying personal goodbyes as people start to leave.
wind_down.script: Hey everyone — this has been such a good night and I am so glad you all came. We are going to start wrapping up, so finish your drinks, grab anything you need, and thank you genuinely for being here.
